Same
SAYM
interjection (Millennial slang)
The ordinary adjective same used alone as a reply meaning "I feel exactly the same" or "that is me too." It became common on Tumblr and Twitter in the early 2010s as a response to relatable posts ("Same."), along with mood, big mood, relatable, and me. The one-word reply is a gesture of fellow-feeling: I recognize myself in what you said.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

"Same" is the one-word reply that means "me too": you posted that you are tired, overwhelmed, craving pizza, or awkward at parties, and a friend writes, simply, "same." It is a small act of solidarity. The Christian observation: there is something precious in the impulse, and the gospel knows it well. Human beings are comforted to learn that they are not alone in their struggles. Paul writes, "There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man" (1Co 10:13). The Church is meant to be a community where people can say "same" about their weaknesses and find company. "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep" (Rom 12:15). Above all, the Lord Jesus is the great "same" of the gospel: "For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin" (Heb 4:15). He became like us so that He could help us. There is also an ultimate Same in Scripture: "Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever" (Heb 13:8). The only caution is that "same" can stop at recognition and never move to help or change; shared complaint can become a club for staying stuck. A father welcomes his children’s honesty about struggle, says "same" when it is true, and then points them to the One who was tempted like us and can lift us.

Webster 1828 Definition

Millennial one-word reply (early 2010s Tumblr and Twitter) meaning "I feel the same"; a small solidarity the gospel deepens: temptations common to man (1Co 10:13), a High Priest touched with our infirmities (Heb 4:15).

Decode for parents: "same" is fellow-feeling; help it move from shared complaint to shared help.

Key Scripture

1Co 10:13 — "There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it."

Rom 12:15 — "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep."

Heb 4:15 — "For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin."

Heb 13:8 — "Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever."

Gal 6:2 — "Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ."

Modern Corruption

Same is a small, good solidarity; its only drift is shared complaint that never moves to help or change, which Scripture answers with burden-bearing and a High Priest who helps.

expand to see more

The small drift in "same" is solidarity without movement. Online, relatability is currency, and posts that confess weakness collect "same" after "same" until weakness becomes an identity and a bonding ritual. A community of "same" can become a support group for staying the same. Real fellowship recognizes struggle and then helps: "Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ" (Gal 6:2).

The redemption is that Christ’s "same" moves. He became the same as us in every way except sin so that He could rescue us, not merely sympathize. Teach the young to admit their weaknesses honestly, to tell friends "me too" when it helps them feel less alone, and then to say, "let’s pray about it," or "here’s what helped me." And teach them the Same who never changes: Jesus Christ, yesterday, today, and for ever.
